title: Relational & logical operators
learningGoals: use ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= and know each gives 1 (true) or 0 (false)

youtube.title: True or False, No Maybe: == && || ! | C Programming EP 16
youtube.description: In C, every comparison answers with a number: 1 for true, 0 for false. This episode covers all six relational operators and the three logical ones (AND, OR, NOT), shows short-circuiting, and catches the most famous bug in C: one equals sign instead of two. 0:00 True or false, no maybe · 0:20 1 means true, 0 means false · 1:00 The six comparisons · 2:20 AND, OR, NOT · 3:05 Code: can you board the bus? · 4:00 Short-circuiting · 4:34 Bug of the Day: = vs == · 5:24 Challenge · 6:09 Next episode

chapters.label: Code: can you board the bus?

thumbnail.visual: big text "= OR ==?" in apricot on cream; one equals sign in tomato with a cross, two equals signs in mint with a tick; Xecxec squinting between them.

scenes.onScreen: Question cards "Is it raining?", "Is the bus here?", "Maybe?"
scenes.animation: First two cards flip to 1 and 0 with a ding each; the "Maybe?" card gets stamped "NOT IN C" in tomato with a thud; Xecxec shakes his head, claw-click
scenes.narration: Is it raining? Yes or no. Is the bus here? Yes or no. Maybe? Not in C. In C, every question has exactly two answers. True or false. No maybe.

scenes.animation: Title stamps in on cream with whoosh + thud; apricot underline wipe

scenes.onScreen: A light switch: ON = 1 = true, OFF = 0 = false; six operator tiles: == != < > <= >=
scenes.animation: Switch flips with a click sound and the bulb lights; tiles pop in with marimba notes; == tile gets a "TWO equals" label
scenes.narration: First, how C says true and false. When you compare two things, C answers with a number. 1 means true. 0 means false. Like a light switch: on or off. Now the six comparison operators, also called relational operators. Double equals: is equal to. Exclamation equals: is not equal to. Less than. Greater than. Less than or equal to. Greater than or equal to. Notice the first one: equal to is written with two equals signs, not one. Remember that. It comes back later in this episode.

scenes.onScreen: rel.c lines 1–10 with tracker and mini terminal
scenes.animation: [HL n] per line; [TRACK] boxes for tide and age; each result 1 or 0 drops into the terminal, 1s in mint with a ding, 0s in tomato with a soft thud
scenes.narration: Let's try them. [HL 4] int tide equals 3, the tide level in metres at Calangute. [TRACK tide=3] [HL 5] int age equals 19. [TRACK age=19] [HL 7] tide double-equals 3: is tide equal to 3? Yes, so this prints 1. [HL 8] tide not-equal 3: is tide different from 3? No, so 0. [HL 9] age greater-than-or-equal 18: 19 is at least 18, so 1. [HL 10] age less-than 13: 19 is not less than 13, so 0. Every comparison becomes a 1 or a 0, and percent d prints it like any other int.

code.output:
tide == 3  -> 1
tide != 3  -> 0
age >= 18  -> 1
age < 13   -> 0
can board  -> 1
weekend or holiday -> 1
!hasTicket -> 0

scenes.narration: Real questions often have more than one part. For that, C has three logical operators. Double ampersand means AND: true only when both sides are true. Double pipe, the two vertical lines, means OR: true when at least one side is true. And a single exclamation mark means NOT: it flips true to false and false to true. Look at the tables. For AND, only one box out of four is true: both yes. For OR, three boxes are true: only both no gives false.

scenes.onScreen: rel.c lines 12–19: bus boarding with a small Kadamba-style bus illustration
scenes.animation: [HL n] per line; [TRACK] boxes hasTicket and busFull; bus door opens with a hiss SFX when the result is 1
scenes.narration: Now a bus question. [HL 12] int hasTicket equals 1, so yes, you have a ticket. [TRACK hasTicket=1] [HL 13] int busFull equals 0, so the bus is not full. [TRACK busFull=0] [HL 15] Can you board? hasTicket AND not busFull. Not busFull flips 0 into 1. So it's 1 AND 1, which gives 1. Door opens. [HL 16] Weekend or holiday? 0 OR 1. Only one side needs to be true, so 1. [HL 17] Not hasTicket: not 1 is 0. [HL 18] Return zero.

code.output:
tide == 3  -> 1
tide != 3  -> 0
age >= 18  -> 1
age < 13   -> 0
can board  -> 1
weekend or holiday -> 1
!hasTicket -> 0

scenes.animation: [HL 5] left side turns tomato 0; right side greys out with a "SKIPPED" stamp and a whoosh; a "divide by zero" bomb icon fizzles out harmlessly
scenes.narration: One clever detail. [HL 4] Here x is 0. [HL 5] We ask: x is not 0, AND 10 divided by x is more than 1. Dividing by zero would crash the program. But it never happens. The left side, x not equal to 0, is already false. With AND, if the left side is false, the answer must be false, so C skips the right side completely. This is called short-circuiting. OR does the same in reverse: if the left side is already true, C skips the right side. [HL 6] So r is 0, and nothing crashes.

scenes.onScreen: "Why did = fail the exam? It copied the answer instead of checking it."
scenes.animation: Card flips, rimshot; Xecxec covers his eyes
scenes.narration: Why did the single equals sign fail the exam? It copied the answer instead of checking it.

scenes.onScreen: marks.c using `marks = 100` instead of `marks == 100`; wrong output
scenes.animation: Butter banner + siren blip; marks tracker box is overwritten from 20 to 100 with a splash SFX; output shown in tomato with a buzzer; second = slides in, output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: And here's the bug that pun was about. [HL 4] marks is 20. [TRACK marks=20] [HL 6] You want to ask: is marks equal to 100? But you type one equals sign. GCC gives no error and no warning here. The program prints: Is it 100? 100. And then: marks is now 100. [TRACK marks=100] One equals sign doesn't compare. It assigns. It puts 100 into marks, and the whole expression has the value 100. Your student just got full marks for free. Fix: two equals signs. Now it prints 0, false, and marks stays 20. Read it aloud as "is equal to" every time you write double equals.

scenes.onScreen: "Is age between 18 and 60?" with a number line, 18 and 60 marked
scenes.animation: Number line draws in; a marker slides along with a whirr; bracket region glows apricot
scenes.narration: Your challenge: read an age with scanf, and print 1 if the age is between 18 and 60, including both, and 0 if not. You need two comparisons and one logical operator. Which one, AND or OR? Comment your line of code.

scenes.onScreen: Next: EP 17 · Increment, decrement, assignment + subscribe
scenes.animation: Next card slides up; Xecxec waves, claw-click; sign-off types in
scenes.narration: Next episode: plus plus, minus minus, and the drama between i plus plus and plus plus i. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
No compile error and no warning, even with -Wall. Wrong output:

Is it 100? 100
marks is now 100
bug.why: = stores a value and evaluates to it, while == compares and evaluates to 1 or 0; inside an if condition (EP 20) GCC with -Wall at least warns "suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value".

pun: "Why did the single equals sign fail the exam? It copied the answer instead of checking it."
challenge: Read an age and print 1 if it is between 18 and 60 (both included), otherwise 0.
challengeAnswer: shown at the start of EP 17. Use AND, because both conditions must be true.

shorts.title: True or false, no maybe
shorts.script: In C, maybe doesn't exist. Is it raining? 1 or 0. Is the bus here? 1 or 0. Every question in C has exactly two answers: 1 for true, 0 for false. Learn the operators that ask those questions in the full episode.
shorts.caption: C has no maybe. Only 1 and 0.

shorts.title: AND, OR, NOT in 30 seconds
shorts.hook: "Can you board the bus? C decides with two symbols."
shorts.script: Can you board the bus? C decides with two symbols. Double ampersand is AND: both sides must be true. Double pipe is OR: at least one side must be true. Exclamation mark is NOT: it flips true and false. hasTicket AND not busFull: 1 AND not 0, which is 1 AND 1. True. Door opens.
shorts.caption: Logical operators explained with a Goa bus.

shorts.title: One = changed the marks
shorts.hook: "This code gave a student full marks for free."
shorts.script: This code gave a student full marks for free. marks was 20. We wanted to ask: is marks equal to 100? But we typed one equals sign. One equals assigns. Now marks is 100. No error, no warning. Fix: two equals signs to compare.
shorts.caption: The most famous one-character bug in C.

shorts.title: The copy-cat equals sign
shorts.script: Why did the single equals sign fail the exam? It copied the answer instead of checking it.
shorts.caption: Xecxec can't look.

shorts.title: Does this crash?
shorts.hook: "x is 0. We divide by x. Does it crash?"
shorts.script: x is 0. This line divides 10 by x. Does the program crash? Comment yes or no. Answer: no. The left side, x not equal to 0, is false, so AND skips the right side completely. That's called short-circuiting.
shorts.caption: Crash or no crash? Comment before the answer.
